Ryan — thanks, this is helpful. Attaching an initial one-pager and an XLS (see attachments) with the rough tokenization walk-forward. High level notes up-front:

- Baseline tokens/sec derived from our benchmark on 13B-int8 on A100p4: 13B -> ~9.6k tokens/sec per GPU under continuous batching for short-turns (120 tokens); for long-turns average throughput per GPU drops ~45%.
- We apply a derating factor for mixed workloads and multi-tenant interference: recommended starting derate = 0.78 (22% slack). This accounts for KV cache cold starts, NVLink scheduling jitter, and headroom for autoscaling bursts.
- For Nexus's mix (70/30 short/long) we estimate effective tokens/sec per GPU = ~7.5k tokens/sec.
- To meet p95 <= 600ms at peak (220 qps), we recommend a committed slab equal to the 99% demand percentile + 25% runway. That maps to: 220 qps * avg tokens per request (we conservatively use 260 tokens) = ~57.2k tokens/sec required at peak. After derating and runway => commit target ~95k tokens/sec equivalent capacity.

I've looped in Ben (SE) and Priyom (Infra) for the slab math and latency mapping — Ben, can you add a short slab allocation and latency budget table? Priyom, any callouts re: cache warmup tuning or quantization caveats?

Best,
Priya

Folks — quick slab breakdown and latency budget (summary):

- Assumptions: 13B-int8 performance numbers from our internal benching (A100p4): short-turns 9.6k t/s, long-turns 5.3k t/s. Mixed-weight effective = 0.7*9.6k + 0.3*5.3k = 8.65k t/s; apply Priya derate 0.78 -> ~6.75k t/s per GPU.

- Slab sizing: Redwood slabs are billed as groups of 8 GPUs. Effective slab capacity = 8 * 6.75k = 54k tokens/sec.

- Nexus target (95k tokens/sec) -> allocate 2 slabs (16 GPUs) = 108k tokens/sec effective. That gives ~13% runway above the 95k target and aligns with our minimum slit/failover pattern for redundant NVLink domains.

- Latency budget: with 16 GPUs and continuous batching (max batch window 15ms) we model p50 ~120ms, p95 ~480–560ms depending on long-turn KV misses. The tail is dominated by KV warmups for long sessions (cache cold misses add 80–210ms depending on session length).

- Operational recommendations: enable prefix KV warmup for known active users, pre-warm common prompts during expected peak windows, and configure autoscaling burst to add a single additional slab (8 GPUs) on sustained >85% utilization for >5 minutes.

I'll attach a short table mapping slab count -> tokens/sec -> expected p95. If Nexus wants a tighter SLA (p95 <= 400ms) we either need a second 8-GPU slab for dedicated low-latency lanes or prioritize lower batch windows at the cost of token efficiency.

-Ben

Adding engineering nuance — Priya/Ben:

- Derating: our 0.78 number is reasonable for early ramp but split sources: NVLink saturation (7–10%), KV cache cold misses (8–12% averaged across sessions), scheduling jitter & infra noise (3–5%). If Nexus will accept a warm cache strategy and sticky routing (session pinning) we can push derate to 0.85 after first 30 days.

- Quantization: 13B-int8 has ~5–8% slower decode on some kernels vs int4 quant+QKV fusion; we measured throughput variance across sequence length. Recommend we validate their precise prompt mix in a 48-hour soak to refine slab commitment.

- Headroom policy: implement a 2-stage headroom: (1) Billing commit = 2 slabs (as Ben recommended), (2) Operational safety buffer: soft auto-burst to a 3rd slab for 3–10 minute spikes; this keeps p95 under 600ms without forcing permanent commit.

- KV cache strategy: pre-warm top 5% of prompts via a scheduled background warmup job (we can supply the script) and enable shared KV across GPU domains where possible.

- Test plan before commit: 48hr soak with synthetic mix (70/30) and a web-traffic replay of their logs; provide results and a one-time commit adjustment.

Cheers,
Priyom Das
Lead Inference Engineer, Redwood Inference
